a: Python's main features: it is dynamically typed (no type declarations needed), interpreted (runs line by line), and has a clean, readable syntax that makes it fast to learn. It is multi-paradigm (object-oriented, functional, procedural), has a huge standard library ('batteries included'), automatic memory management, and thousands of third-party packages (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn). It is cross-platform and has strong community support, which is why it dominates data science and ML.

The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) is a mutex in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, even on multi-core CPUs. It simplifies memory management but limits CPU-bound multithreading. Workarounds: multiprocessing (separate processes, each with its own GIL), native libraries like NumPy that release the GIL during heavy computation, or async for I/O-bound work.

A list is mutable (you can add, remove, or change items after creation) while a tuple is immutable (fixed once created). Tuples are slightly faster, use less memory, and can be dictionary keys because they are hashable; lists cannot. Use a list for a collection that changes over time, and a tuple for fixed records like coordinates (x, y) or when you need hashability.

A Python dictionary is a hash map: each key is run through a hash function, and the hash determines where the value is stored in memory, so lookup, insert, and delete are O(1) on average. Keys must be hashable (strings, numbers, tuples), and since Python 3.7 dictionaries preserve insertion order. Collisions are handled internally with open addressing.

A list comprehension is a compact one-line way to build a list: [x*x for x in nums if x > 0] squares every positive element. It is usually faster and more readable than an equivalent for-loop with append. Use it for simple transforms; switch to a normal loop when logic gets complex, because readability wins.

A decorator is a function that takes another function and extends its behavior without modifying its code, applied with the @ syntax. Common uses: logging, timing, caching (functools.lru_cache), authentication checks, and retry logic. It works because functions are first-class objects in Python — they can be passed around and returned like any value.

A generator is a function that uses yield to produce values one at a time, lazily, instead of building the whole list in memory. Each next() call resumes the function right after the last yield, keeping its state. This makes generators memory-efficient for huge datasets or infinite sequences — a big deal in data pipelines where you stream batches instead of loading everything.

A shallow copy (copy.copy or list[:]) creates a new outer object but inserts references to the same inner objects, so changing a nested item affects both copies. A deep copy (copy.deepcopy) recursively clones every level, making a fully independent duplicate. Use deep copy when you mutate nested structures and must not touch the original.

Python handles errors with try/except blocks: risky code goes in try, and specific exception types (ValueError, KeyError) are caught in except so one failure does not crash the program. else runs when no exception occurred, finally always runs (cleanup like closing files). Best practice: catch specific exceptions, never a bare except, and raise custom exceptions for domain errors.

OOP in Python rests on four pillars: encapsulation (bundling data and methods in a class, hiding internals), inheritance (a child class reuses and extends a parent class), polymorphism (the same method call works on different classes, e.g. every model object has .predict()), and abstraction (exposing only what matters). Python supports multiple inheritance and magic (dunder) methods like __init__ and __str__ to customize behavior.

NumPy is much faster than Python lists because arrays are contiguous blocks of one fixed dtype (like C arrays) with no per-element object overhead, and operations run as compiled C loops over the whole array at once — that is vectorization. It also supports broadcasting (operating on arrays of different shapes without copying), which replaces slow Python loops with clean, fast array math.

Broadcasting is NumPy's set of rules for operating on arrays of different shapes without copying data: dimensions are compared right to left, and an array is virtually stretched if a dimension is 1 or missing. Example: adding a (3,1) column vector to a (1,4) row vector produces a (3,4) matrix. It makes code concise and avoids slow loops.

pandas provides two core structures: a Series (a one-dimensional labeled array) and a DataFrame (a two-dimensional table of columns, each possibly a different dtype, with a row index). It is built on NumPy, so operations are vectorized. DataFrames are the workhorse of data science: reading files, cleaning, filtering, joining, and aggregating data before modeling.

loc selects rows/columns by label (df.loc['row5', 'age']), and slicing with loc is inclusive of the endpoint. iloc selects by integer position (df.iloc[3, 0]), and slicing is exclusive like normal Python. Rule of thumb: loc when you know names, iloc when you know positions — mixing them up is a classic source of off-by-one bugs.

groupby follows split-apply-combine: it splits rows into groups by key, applies an aggregation (mean, sum, count, or a custom function) to each group, and combines the results into a new table. Example: df.groupby('department')['salary'].mean() gives the average salary per department. It is the pandas equivalent of SQL GROUP BY and the main tool for aggregated analysis.

merge joins two DataFrames on common columns like SQL (how='inner'/'left'/'right'/'outer'), join is merge keyed on indexes, and concat stacks DataFrames vertically (axis=0) or side by side (axis=1). Use merge for relational combines (orders + customers on customer_id), concat for appending monthly files into one table.

Missing values are handled by first understanding why they are missing, then either dropping (dropna — only if few rows or the column is mostly empty) or imputing: mean/median for numeric (median when skewed or with outliers), mode for categorical, 'Unknown' category, or model-based imputation like KNN Imputer. Never fill blindly — wrong imputation silently biases the model, and always add a 'was_missing' indicator flag when missingness itself can be predictive.

apply runs a Python function row by row (or column by column), which is flexible but slow because it drops back to Python-level looping. Vectorized operations (df['b'] = df['a'] * 2, np.where, replace, map on a dict) run in optimized C and are typically 10-100x faster. Rule: always try a vectorized solution first; reach for apply only when the logic truly cannot be expressed vectorized.

SQL joins combine rows from two tables on a key: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows in both; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows plus matches (NULLs where none); RIGHT JOIN is the mirror; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps everything from both. Cross join is every combination. In interviews, mention that LEFT JOIN + WHERE right IS NULL is the classic way to find rows with no match.

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. So 'WHERE salary > 50000' removes low earners first, while 'HAVING COUNT(*) > 5' keeps only departments with more than five people. You cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE — that is exactly what HAVING exists for.

An index is a data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table, turning full-table O(n) lookups into O(log n). Trade-off: indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and use storage. Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY; a clustered index dictates physical row order (one per table), non-clustered are separate lookup structures.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table (no NULLs, no duplicates, one per table). A foreign key is a column in another table that references a primary key, enforcing referential integrity — you cannot point to a customer that does not exist. Together they are the backbone of relational design: one customer row, many order rows linked by customer_id.

Database normalization organizes tables to remove redundancy and anomalies: 1NF — atomic values, no repeating groups; 2NF — every non-key column depends on the whole key; 3NF — no transitive dependencies (column depending on another non-key column). Benefit: updates happen in one place. Data-warehouse/analytics tables are often deliberately denormalized (star schema) to avoid expensive joins at read time.

DELETE removes rows one by one with a WHERE filter, is logged, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows instantly by deallocating pages — much faster, no WHERE, and typically resets identity counters. DROP removes the entire table structure (data and schema). Order of destruction: DELETE for selective removal, TRUNCATE to empty, DROP to erase.

UNION combines results of two queries and removes duplicates (it internally does a distinct sort, which costs time); UNION ALL keeps everything, including duplicates, and is faster. Use UNION ALL whenever duplicates are impossible or acceptable — it is the performance-friendly default.

Window functions compute aggregates across a set of rows while keeping every row visible — unlike GROUP BY, which collapses them. Syntax: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers employees within each department by salary. Common uses: top-N per group, running totals, and the classic deduplication pattern (delete where row_number > 1). RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not.

To find duplicates: GROUP BY the columns that define a duplicate, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. To remove them while keeping one copy, use a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id), then delete rows where the number is greater than 1. In pandas the equivalent is df.drop_duplicates(subset=[...]).

The classic 'second highest salary' has three answers: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp); or with DISTINCT + OFFSET: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1; or a window function with DENSE_RANK. Mentioning all three and their edge cases (ties, NULLs) is what impresses in an interview.

A CTE (WITH clause) is a named temporary result set that makes complex queries readable and allows referencing the same intermediate result multiple times — recursive CTEs can even walk hierarchies (org charts, bill of materials). A correlated subquery references the outer query's row and runs once per row, which is powerful but slow — often a JOIN or window function is faster.

Variance measures average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation is its square root, bringing the spread back into the original units (salary in rupees, not rupees-squared). Population variance divides by N, sample variance by N-1 (Bessel's correction) to avoid underestimating spread from a sample. High variance means data points are widely scattered around the mean.

Correlation measures that two variables move together (from -1 to +1); causation means one actually changes the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings correlate — summer drives both, that is a confounder. Correlation alone never proves causation: you need experiments (A/B tests) or causal methods (controls, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences) to claim cause and effect.

Covariance measures how two variables vary together but is unbounded and unit-dependent, so its magnitude is hard to compare across pairs. Correlation (Pearson) is covariance divided by both standard deviations, normalizing it to [-1, 1] and making it scale-invariant: correlation between kg and pounds is the same value. Use covariance for math inside models, correlation for communication and feature analysis.

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the symmetric bell curve defined by its mean and standard deviation. Its key property is the empirical rule: about 68% of data falls within 1 standard deviation, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3. It matters because averages of many independent effects tend toward it (CLT), and many statistical tests assume normality of residuals.

Skewness measures asymmetry: positive (right) skew has a long right tail — income, house prices — where mean > median; negative (left) skew is the mirror. Kurtosis measures tail heaviness (how extreme outliers can be). Practical impact: skew skews the mean and hurts linear-model assumptions, so apply log or Box-Cox transforms to strongly skewed features.

The Central Limit Theorem says that for a large enough sample size, the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution no matter the population's shape. It is the foundation of inference: it is why confidence intervals and hypothesis tests on means work, why the sampling distribution's standard error is sigma/sqrt(n), and why n >= 30 is the usual rule of thumb.

Standardization (z-score) centers data at mean 0 with standard deviation 1 — robust to outliers, keeps relative spacing, and is the default for algorithms like SVM, logistic regression, and PCA. Min-max normalization squeezes values into [0,1] — bounded, but a single outlier compresses everything else. Scale after the train/test split, fitting the scaler on train only, to avoid leakage.

Bayes' theorem updates a belief with evidence: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B) — posterior = likelihood times prior over evidence. Example: a rare disease test with 99% accuracy still yields mostly false positives when the disease prevalence is 1 in 1000, because the tiny prior dominates. It is the mathematical heart of Naive Bayes, spam filters, and medical-test reasoning.

Key distributions: Bernoulli — one yes/no trial; Binomial — number of successes in n trials (coin flips); Poisson — counts of events per interval (calls per hour at a call center); Exponential — time between Poisson events; Uniform — equal likelihood; Normal — the bell curve. Choosing the right one means matching what is being counted or measured: successes, counts per time, gaps between events.

The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. p = 0.03 means: under no-effect, results this strong happen 3% of the time — it is NOT the probability the null is true, and NOT the size of the effect. Small p + small effect can still be meaningless; always pair significance with effect size and practical relevance.

A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null (convicting an innocent person) — its probability is alpha, the significance level. A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject a false null (letting a guilty person go) — its probability is beta, and power = 1 - beta. Which is worse depends on cost: for a cancer test you tolerate more false positives; for a spam filter the reverse.

A 95% confidence interval gives a range that would contain the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples — [104, 116] for a mean of 110. Width grows with variability and confidence level, shrinks with sample size. It is more honest than a point estimate because it shows uncertainty, and if the interval for a difference straddles zero, the effect is not significant at that level.

Hypothesis testing: state H0 (no effect) and H1, pick significance level alpha, choose the test — t-test/z-test for comparing means (z when sigma known or n large, t for small samples), chi-square for categorical associations, ANOVA for 3+ group means — compute the statistic, get the p-value, and reject H0 if p < alpha. Always also report the effect size; significance without magnitude is not actionable.

Sampling studies a subset to infer about a population: simple random gives every unit equal chance; stratified divides into strata (male/female, regions) and samples within each — guaranteeing representation; cluster samples whole groups (schools, villages) for cost; systematic takes every k-th unit; convenience sampling is biased but common. Bad sampling is the most common root of wrong conclusions.

Overfitting is when a model learns noise instead of signal — near-perfect on training data, poor on unseen data. Underfitting is too simple to capture the pattern — bad everywhere. Diagnosis: large train-validation gap means overfit; both scores low means underfit. Fixes for overfitting: more data, regularization (L1/L2), simpler model, fewer features, early stopping, dropout, ensembling; for underfitting: bigger model, better features, less regularization.

Bias is error from wrong assumptions — an overly simple model systematically misses the pattern (high bias, underfit). Variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample — a complex model changes wildly with different data (high variance, overfit). Total error = bias squared + variance + irreducible noise, and tuning model complexity is exactly walking the trade-off: decrease one, increase the other, minimize the sum.

Regularization adds a penalty on coefficient size to the loss so the model cannot chase noise. L2 (Ridge) shrinks weights smoothly toward zero — good default, handles multicollinearity. L1 (Lasso) drives some weights exactly to zero, doing automatic feature selection and giving sparse, interpretable models. Elastic Net mixes both. The strength (alpha/C) is a hyperparameter tuned by cross-validation.

Cross-validation splits data into k folds, trains on k-1 and validates on the remaining fold, rotating until every fold has been the validator, then averages the scores. It gives a far more reliable performance estimate than a single split and exposes instability. Variants: StratifiedKFold keeps class ratios (use for imbalanced data), GroupKFold prevents leakage across grouped rows, TimeSeriesSplit respects time order.

Data is split into train (fit parameters), validation (tune hyperparameters, choose models), and test (final, untouched estimate — used once). The test set must simulate the future: never leak into training, and with time-series data the split must be chronological, not random. A common ratio is 70/15/15 or 80/20 with cross-validation playing the validation role.

A decision tree splits data by asking yes/no questions, choosing at each node the feature and threshold that maximize purity — measured by Gini impurity or entropy/information gain. It is interpretable (you can draw it) and needs no scaling, but a full tree overfits badly, so we constrain depth, min samples per leaf, or prune. Trees are also the building blocks of Random Forest and all gradient boosting models.

Random Forest trains many decision trees on bootstrap samples of the data and averages their votes (bagging). Two randomness sources decorrelate the trees: each tree sees a random data sample, and each split considers a random subset of features. Result: variance drops dramatically versus one tree. It is robust, handles nonlinearities, gives feature importances, and needs little tuning — a strong baseline.

Bagging trains models independently in parallel on random samples and averages them — it reduces variance (Random Forest). Boosting trains models sequentially, each new model focusing on the previous ones' mistakes — it reduces bias (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost). Bagging is easy to parallelize and hard to overfit; boosting is often more accurate but needs careful tuning and can overfit noisy data.

Gradient boosting builds trees one at a time, each new tree fitting the residual errors (negative gradients) of the current ensemble, then all trees sum their predictions. XGBoost/LightGBM add regularization, clever split-finding, and column sampling, making it the go-to for tabular-data competitions. Key hyperparameters: learning rate (smaller + more trees = better), tree depth, subsampling.

An SVM finds the hyperplane that maximizes the margin — the distance to the nearest points of each class (the support vectors). The kernel trick (RBF, polynomial) implicitly maps data into higher dimensions so non-linear boundaries become linear — no explicit feature engineering. C controls the tolerance for misclassification (small C = wider margin, more slack). SVMs shine on small-to-medium, high-dimensional datasets; they scale poorly to millions of rows.

KNN classifies a point by the majority vote of its k nearest neighbors (or averages them for regression) — there is no training phase, all the work happens at prediction, so it is called lazy learning. Distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan) matters, features must be scaled, and small k overfits while large k oversmooths (odd k avoids ties in binary problems). It struggles in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality) and is slow on big data.

Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem with a 'naive' assumption: features are independent given the class. That makes training just counting frequencies — extremely fast, works with tiny data, and shines on text classification (spam, sentiment) where word counts are features (Multinomial NB). Despite the unrealistic independence assumption it performs surprisingly well; zero-frequency problems are handled by Laplace smoothing.

Linear regression fits y = b0 + b1x1 + ... by minimizing squared errors (OLS). Its assumptions: linearity of the relationship, independent errors, constant error variance (homoscedasticity), normal residuals (for inference), and no severe multicollinearity among features — check with VIF. Coefficients are interpretable: 'one more year of experience adds 8,000 to salary, holding education constant'. Outliers pull OLS hard because errors are squared.

Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier: it linearly combines features, passes the result through a sigmoid, and outputs a probability between 0 and 1, thresholded (usually 0.5) into classes. It is trained with log-loss, gives well-calibrated probabilities, and coefficients are interpretable as log-odds. It is the industry baseline for binary problems — fast, explainable, and surprisingly hard to beat on structured data.

K-means clusters by alternating two steps: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its members, repeating until stable. You must choose k — the elbow method (plot inertia vs k) or silhouette score helps. It assumes roughly spherical, similar-size clusters and is sensitive to initialization (k-means++ fixes this) and to outliers; scale features first. DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering handles non-spherical shapes better.

Hierarchical clustering builds a tree (dendrogram) of nested clusters — agglomerative starts with single points and merges the closest pairs; cut the tree at a height to get k clusters, no need to fix k in advance. DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions separated by sparse space: no k needed, finds arbitrary shapes, and labels outliers as noise — but it struggles when cluster densities differ.

PCA finds new orthogonal axes (principal components) ordered by how much variance they capture, then keeps the top ones — compressing, say, 50 correlated features into 5 components holding 90% of the variance. It is unsupervised, requires centered (usually standardized) data, and components are linear mixes of original features, so interpretability drops. Uses: visualization in 2D, noise reduction, speeding up training, fighting the curse of dimensionality.

Distance- and gradient-based algorithms need features on comparable scales: KNN, SVM, K-means, PCA, and all gradient-descent models (linear/logistic, neural nets) — otherwise a feature in thousands dominates one in fractions. Tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost) split by thresholds per feature and are scale-invariant — no scaling needed. Fit the scaler on training data only and apply it to validation/test.

Categorical features become numbers before modeling: one-hot encoding makes a binary column per category (safe for linear models and neural nets, but explodes with high cardinality); label/ordinal encoding maps to integers (fine for tree models, but imposes fake order for linear models); target encoding replaces a category with the mean of the target — powerful for hundreds of categories but must be done inside cross-validation to avoid leakage. High cardinality is where target encoding or frequency encoding earns its keep.

Interaction features combine existing ones to capture joint effects a linear model cannot: price times quantity, age times income, or polynomial terms like x-squared. Create them when domain logic suggests the effect of one feature depends on another (ad spend interacts with season). Tree models discover many interactions automatically; linear models need them hand-built. Beware: they multiply feature count fast and raise overfitting risk — validate their value.

Feature selection keeps only the features that earn their place: filter methods score features statistically (correlation, chi-square, mutual information) independent of any model; wrapper methods search subsets by actually training models (RFE — recursive feature elimination) — accurate but expensive; embedded methods do it during training (Lasso's L1 zeros, tree feature importances). Benefits: less overfitting, faster training, simpler explanations.

For imbalanced classes: resample (oversample the minority with SMOTE, which creates synthetic points between real neighbors; or undersample the majority), use class weights so errors on the rare class cost more, and pick thresholds or algorithms that handle it (XGBoost's scale_pos_weight). Critically: never measure with plain accuracy — 99% accuracy is trivial when 99% is majority class. Use precision/recall, F1, or PR-AUC, and split with stratification.

Precision = of everything predicted positive, how many truly are (TP/(TP+FP)) — 'when I alarm, am I right?'. Recall = of all real positives, how many did I catch (TP/(TP+FN)) — 'how much did I miss?'. They trade off via the threshold: raising it raises precision, lowers recall. F1 is their harmonic mean, punishing imbalance between them. Fraud/medical screening favors recall; spam filtering favors precision.

The ROC curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across all thresholds; AUC is the area under it — the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect). With heavy class imbalance the ROC can flatter a weak model, so prefer the Precision-Recall curve and PR-AUC — they focus only on the minority class and are far more honest there.

The confusion matrix is the 2x2 (or NxN) table of predictions vs reality: TP, FP (Type I), FN (Type II), TN. Every metric falls out of it — accuracy = (TP+TN)/all; precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP). Reading the raw matrix is often more informative than any single number: it shows exactly which class the model confuses with which.

Regression metrics: MAE is the mean absolute error — robust, in original units, treats all errors equally; RMSE squares errors first, so big mistakes hurt much more — use it when large errors are disproportionately costly; R-squared is the share of variance explained (1.0 perfect, can go negative on terrible models), and adjusted R-squared penalizes useless extra features. Report MAE and RMSE together: a big gap between them signals outlier-driven errors.

Calibration asks: when the model says 70%, does the event happen about 70% of the time? Many strong models (SVM, boosted trees) rank well but output distorted probabilities. Check with a reliability curve or Brier score; fix with Platt scaling (sigmoid, for small data) or isotonic regression (for large data), always via cross-validation. Calibrated probabilities are essential when decisions use thresholds, pricing, or risk values.

Hyperparameters are settings chosen before training (tree depth, learning rate, regularization strength). Grid search tries every combination — thorough but explodes combinatorially; random search samples configurations and finds good regions far faster (important params get more unique values); Bayesian optimization (Optuna, Hyperopt) learns from past trials which region to sample next. Always tune inside cross-validation, on the validation set only — never the test set.

Data leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training, giving great validation scores and a miserable real world. Classic forms: target leakage (a feature that is a proxy for the outcome — 'refund issued' predicting churn), fitting scalers/imputers/feature selection on the full dataset before splitting, splitting time-ordered data randomly, and group leakage (same customer in train and test). Prevention: split first, pipeline everything, and be suspicious of suspiciously high scores.

The curse of dimensionality: as dimensions grow, data becomes sparse, distances between points concentrate (nearest and farthest neighbor look alike), and models need exponentially more data to fill the space — KNN and K-means degrade first. Remedies: feature selection, PCA or other dimensionality reduction, and algorithms robust to sparsity (trees, linear models with regularization).

An A/B test randomly splits users into control and treatment to measure a change's causal effect: define one primary metric and the minimum detectable effect up front, compute the required sample size (power analysis), run for full weekly cycles to capture behavior rhythms, then compare with a significance test. Sins to avoid: peeking and stopping at p < 0.05 early, running many metrics and cherry-picking, and ignoring novelty effects.

A stationary series has constant mean, variance, and autocorrelation over time — most forecasting models assume it (or something close). Check with the ADF test or by eyeballing trend/seasonality. Achieve stationarity by differencing (removing trend), log transforms (stabilizing variance), and seasonal differencing. Non-stationarity is why naive regression on time data gives nonsense correlations (spurious regression).

ARIMA(p,d,q) forecasts from a series' own past: AR(p) — regression on p previous values; I(d) — difference d times to make it stationary; MA(q) — regression on q previous forecast errors. SARIMA adds seasonal terms; exogenous variables make it SARIMAX. Workflow: decompose the series (trend/seasonality/residual), make stationary, pick orders via ACF/PACF plots or auto-arima, validate on a chronological holdout. Prophet is a robust, interpretable alternative for business series.

Recommenders mainly come in two flavors: collaborative filtering ('users like you also liked...') via user-item matrix factorization — no item knowledge needed but suffers the cold-start problem for new users/items; content-based ('similar items to what you liked') using item features — works cold but creates filter bubbles. Hybrids blend both, often with a candidate-generation + ranking two-stage design. Evaluation uses precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, and online A/B tests.

Causal inference answers 'what happens if we intervene' rather than just predicting. Core tools: randomized experiments (gold standard), difference-in-differences (compare pre/post changes between treatment and control groups), instrumental variables (external shock affecting only treatment), matching/propensity scores (compare similar units), and uplift modeling (predicting who is persuaded by treatment, not just who converts). Correlation adjustments alone never guarantee causality — identification does.

Explainability methods: SHAP assigns each feature a contribution to each prediction using game theory — consistent, local and global views; LIME fits a small local model around one prediction to approximate it; tree models give global feature importances directly; partial dependence and permutation importance show how predictions move as a feature changes. Needed for regulated domains (credit, healthcare), debugging, and stakeholder trust.

ML system design interviews look for end-to-end thinking: clarify the business goal and metric; define the ML task (ranking, classification) and label; data sources and pipeline; features and leakage protection; model choice with a simple baseline first; offline metrics plus online A/B validation; serving design (batch scoring vs real-time API, latency budget, feature store); monitoring for drift and retraining strategy; and fallbacks. Start simple, scale with evidence — naming trade-offs matters more than one 'right' architecture.

MLOps applies DevOps discipline to ML: version control for code, data, and models (DVC, model registry); CI/CD pipelines that test not just code but data and model quality; deployment patterns (shadow, canary, blue-green); monitoring beyond infra — input data drift (distribution shifts) and concept drift (the X-y relationship itself changes, e.g. COVID breaking demand models); automated retraining triggers with human approval gates. A model is not a deliverable; a monitored, retrainable loop is.

A feature store is a system that computes, stores, and serves features consistently for training (historical, point-in-time correct) and inference (low-latency online lookup). Its core promise is eliminating training-serving skew — the silent killer where features are computed slightly differently offline and online, so the model sees different data in each. Examples: Feast, Tecton, SageMaker Feature Store.

Batch pipelines process data on a schedule (nightly scoring, hourly aggregates) — simpler, cheaper, fine when freshness of hours is acceptable. Streaming/real-time processes events as they arrive (Kafka + Flink/Spark Streaming, real-time fraud scoring in milliseconds) — costlier and operationally harder, necessary when decisions must react in seconds. Many production systems are a hybrid: batch for model training, streaming for features and alerts.

ETL extracts data from sources, transforms it (clean, join, aggregate), and loads it into a warehouse; ELT loads raw first and transforms inside the warehouse (the modern pattern with Snowflake/BigQuery, using tools like dbt). Data lakes hold raw unstructured data, warehouses hold modeled analytics tables (star schema), and orchestration tools (Airflow) schedule and monitor the pipelines.

The CAP theorem says a distributed data store can guarantee only two of three: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), and Partition tolerance (survives network splits) — and partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, so in practice you choose between CP (e.g. HBase) and AP (e.g. Cassandra) behavior during a partition.

Data cleaning workflow: profile first (nulls, duplicates, ranges, distributions); fix structural issues (wrong dtypes, inconsistent units and casing, typos in categories); handle duplicates and impossible values (age 200, negative price) by rules or domain confirmation, not blind deletion; treat missingness per the earlier framework; and log every transformation so it is reproducible. Most real projects spend 60-80% of time here — saying that in an interview shows experience.

What separates senior from junior: juniors execute well-defined tasks — pick a model, hit a metric; seniors frame the problem — questioning whether the metric is right, what the decision will be, whether ML is even needed. Seniors think in systems (pipelines, monitoring, failure modes, cost), in trade-offs (complexity vs maintainability), and in stakeholders (communicating uncertainty to non-technical partners). The fastest tell: a senior says 'it depends, and here is what it depends on', then reasons to a decision.
